name: McDonald, J.

name: Oxley, J.
description: Concurred with majority opinion.

name: May, J.

name: McDermott, J.

name: Waterman, J.

name: Christensen, C.J.
description: Dissented with majority opinion.

name: Oxley, J.

name: Christensen, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the district court has a statutory and constitutional obligation to review claims of temporary overload, and that the majority's opinion is self-contradictory and misapplies separation of powers.

name: Mansfield, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's opinion is self-contradictory regarding the "indigent defense crisis" and the "temporary overload" claim, and that the separation of powers doctrine supports the district court's role in reviewing overload claims.

name: Christensen, C.J.

name: May, J.

name: Oxley, J.
description: Dissented with May, J.'s opinion.

name: McDonald, J.
description: Concurred, argued that there is no federal or state constitutional right to carry a firearm while illegally possessing a controlled substance or committing an indictable offense.

name: Mansfield, J.

name: Oxley, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the plurality's broad declaration was unnecessary, but agreed there is no constitutional right to carry a firearm for an unlawful purpose.

name: McDermott, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the plurality's reasoning failed to distinguish between dangerous and nondangerous activities, upholding a firearm restriction without historical tradition.

name: Waterman, J.
description: Dissented with majority opinion.

name: May, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the concurrence failed to require the State to prove an unlawful purpose for carrying the firearm, instead relying on an insufficient 'nexus' analysis.

name: OXLEY, JUSTICE
description: Concurred, argued that the fanny pack was immediately associated with Scullark's person at the time of arrest, making the search valid as a search incident to arrest without further justification.

name: McDermott, Justice

description: Concurred, argued that Cole waived his Second Amendment and Iowa Constitution Article I, Section 1A rights by voluntarily agreeing to the protective order that prohibited firearm possession.

name: Christensen, C.J.

name: McDonald, J.
description: Concurred with majority opinion.

name: May, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Cole did not waive his Second Amendment rights, citing Supreme Court precedents and the lack of an express judicial finding of dangerousness in the consent order.

name: Oxley, J.
description: Dissented with majority opinion.

name: McDermott, J.
description: Dissented with majority opinion.

name: May, J.
description: Concurred, argued that sovereign immunity dictates the proper outcome, barring money damages claims against the state and its employees for wrongful imprisonment, and that the legislature can modify common law.

name: Christensen, C.J.

name: Waterman, J.
description: Concurred with majority opinion.

name: Mansfield, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the dissents' approach would effectively revive Godfrey through a common law action, which is unworkable and disregards the legislature's authority to modify common law, and that pre-ITCA law did not allow such suits against state officials.

name: McDonald, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the state's extension of sovereign immunity to its officials for false imprisonment is illegal and void as it contravenes the state constitution's structure and text, which secures the right to liberty and remedies for its violation.

name: Oxley, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority wrongly relies on Wagner v. State to extend sovereign immunity to state employees, and that common law false imprisonment claims against state employees are protected by the constitution.

name: McDermott, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the legislature lacks the power to eliminate the common law right to pursue a false imprisonment claim against state officials, as this right is fundamental and embedded in the constitution.

name: Waterman, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Iowa Code section 808.16(3) constitutionally deems curbside garbage abandoned property, thus removing constitutional protection against warrantless searches, and that this is consistent with prior precedent.

name: McDermott, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the legislature cannot define constitutional rights and that people retain a reasonable expectation of privacy in their trash, making warrantless searches unconstitutional.

name: McDermott, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the supreme court possessed emergency powers to toll the statute of limitations during the pandemic, falling within its judicial power and explicit authority to exercise supervisory and administrative control over the court system.

name: Christensen, C.J.

name: Waterman, J.
description: Concurred with majority opinion.

name: Mansfield, J.
description: Concurred with majority opinion.

name: McDonald, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the court's equitable power to toll statutes of limitations in extraordinary circumstances, like the pandemic, was a constitutional exercise of power, though for reasons different from the majority.

name: Oxley, J.
description: Concurred with Justice McDonald's opinion.

name: May, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the supreme court lacked the power to revise statutes of limitations, as that power belongs to the legislature, and the court's supervisory, administrative, or inherent authorities do not permit such revisions.

name: McDonald, J.
description: Concurred, argued that LULAC lacked standing because it did not assert a legally cognizable injury, as its alleged harms were generalized grievances or discretionary expenditures not directly caused by an infringement of its legal rights.

name: Mansfield, J.

name: McDonald, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the drug dog's brief touch and de minimis intrusion into the vehicle cabin did not violate the Fourth Amendment or Article I, Section 8, and that there was sufficient circumstantial evidence for conviction.

name: Waterman, J.
description: Concurred, delivered the opinion of the court, arguing that Iowa Code section 724.31 is narrowly tailored to serve the compelling state interest of preventing gun violence and suicide, and Amendment 1A does not shift the burden of proof from the petitioner to the State.

name: Christensen, C.J.
description: Concurred with majority opinion.

name: McDonald, J.
description: Concurred in part and concurred in the judgment, arguing that Amendment 1A is inapplicable because Iowa Code section 724.31 is an enlargement or expansion of the right to keep and bear arms, not an infringement or restriction, and state constitutional provisions cannot override federal law.

name: Oxley, J.
description: Concurred with Justice McDonald's separate opinion.

name: McDermott, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority failed to properly apply strict scrutiny, which requires the State to bear the burden of persuasion to prove that the petitioner remains a continuing threat, and that placing the burden on the petitioner means the statute fails strict scrutiny as it is not the least restrictive means.

name: Mansfield, J.
description: Dissented with Justice McDermott's dissenting opinion.

name: May, J.

name: Christensen, C.J.

name: Mansfield, J.

description: Concurred with majority opinion.

name: Waterman, J.
description: Concurred with majority opinion.

name: McDonald, J.
description: Concurred, argued that while the dog sniff was a search under the Iowa Constitution, it was not unlawful under Iowa law, thus not violating Article I, Section 8.

name: May, J.
description: Concurred with Justice McDonald's special concurrence.

name: Oxley, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the dog sniff constituted an unreasonable search under the Fourth Amendment, violating Bauler's rights, as Caballes is irrelevant given Jones and Jardines.

name: McDermott, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the dog sniff violated both the Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution, as the dog's physical intrusion constituted an unreasonable search.

name: MAY, JUSTICE
description: Concurred, argued that the Iowa Constitution guarantees a face-to-face confrontation right requiring two-way visibility, which the one-way video system violated.

name: McDonald, J.

name: Oxley, J.

name: McDermott, J.

name: Christensen, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority strips Iowa women of their bodily autonomy by holding abortion is not a fundamental right, relying on outdated history, and that the statute's exceptions are impractical and harmful, negatively impacting women's health and access to care.

name: Mansfield, J.
description: Dissented, argued that a woman's autonomy over her body is a fundamental right under the Iowa Constitution, that the rational basis test is inappropriate for a near-total abortion ban, and that the six-week ban effectively eliminates the practical ability to have an abortion in Iowa.

name: Waterman, J.
description: Dissented, concurred with Christensen, C.J., and Mansfield, J., dissents.

name: McDonald, Justice.

name: MCDONALD, Justice

name: MANSFIELD, Justice
description: Concurred, agreeing that no liability arises until the city obtains a judgment in district court and that the city's policy of referring unpaid ATE citations to the income tax program without municipal infraction process was improper.

name: OXLEY, JUSTICE
description: Concurred, argued that the district court properly overruled the Batson challenge and correctly found no individual liability for the co-worker, and declined to adopt a higher standard for Batson challenges under the Iowa Constitution.

name: Oxley, J.
description: Recused from the case and took no part in the decision.

name: Waterman, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the court should deny the State's writ of certiorari because the injunction was entered four years ago and not appealed, and the legislature has not reenacted the law. Even if granted, the district court did not act illegally in refusing to dissolve the injunction because the undue burden standard remains the governing law, and the fetal heartbeat bill is unconstitutional under that standard.

name: Susan Larson Christensen, Chief Justice
description: Concurred, agreeing with Justice Waterman's opinion that the court should deny the State's writ of certiorari and that the district court correctly applied the undue burden standard.

name: Mansfield, J.
description: Concurred, agreeing with Justice Waterman's opinion that the court should deny the State's writ of certiorari and that the district court correctly applied the undue burden standard.

name: McDonald, J.
description: Dissented, arguing that the court should grant the State's writ of certiorari, reverse the district court's order, and dissolve the injunction. He contended that the fetal heartbeat law is an actual law, not hypothetical, and that the legal landscape has changed, requiring rational basis review under which the law is constitutional.

name: McDermott, J.
description: Dissented, arguing that the court should grant the State's writ of certiorari and apply the rational basis test, criticizing the majority for refusing to decide the case and for speculating about legislative intent. He joined Justice McDonald's opinion.

name: May, J.
description: Dissented, agreeing with Justice McDonald's opinion that the court should grant the State's writ of certiorari, reverse the district court's order, and dissolve the injunction.

name: May, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act's requirement for equitable proceedings does not violate the constitutional right to a jury trial because the essential nature of CFA civil actions is equitable, and monetary remedies are discretionary and serve remedial purposes.

name: Mansfield, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Godfrey v. State was wrongly decided because it misinterpreted constitutional text and precedent, overlooked important constitutional history, and undermined the established allocation of responsibility between the legislative and judicial branches of government by creating a judicial remedy for constitutional violations without legislative authorization.

name: Christensen, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that overruling Godfrey v. State is justified by its practical unworkability and the need to correct judicial mistakes, consistent with the principles of stare decisis and prior decisions.

name: WATERMAN, Justice

name: McDonald, J.

name: Oxley, J.

All justices joined this opinion.

name: Mansfield, J.
description: Concurred, authored the majority opinion concluding that the 24-hour waiting period did not violate the single-subject rule, issue preclusion did not apply, and PPH II should be overruled.

name: Oxley, J.

name: McDermott, J.
